catalog_quote: As mentioned above, stress affects vowel duration as well as quality. In Belarusian, stress is lexically specified and contrastive (e.g. [ˡkara] ‘punishment; retribution’ vs. [kaˡra] ‘bark (noun)’); it is also used to contrast inflected forms (e.g. [ˡzʲimɨ] ‘winters’ (nom) vs. [zʲiˡmɨ] ‘winter’ (gen). In addition, stress in Belarusian may shift in word-derivation, as in the pair [vos] ‘cart’ vs. [vaˡzɨ] ‘carts’ (Chakhoŭski & Chakhoŭskaya 2010: 51). The primary acoustic correlates of stress are amplitude, pitch and duration. In terms of duration, a three-way contrast is said to exist between stressed, immediately pre-stressed, and unstressed vowels (Padluzhny 2008: 46; Chakhoŭski & Chakhoŭskaya 2010: 52; see also Timberlake 2004: 43–44, on Russian).

new_statements.quote: In Belarusian, as in Russian and Ukrainian, stress may be lexically contrastive, e.g., muká ‘flour’, múka ‘torment’, kása ‘braid’, kasá ‘scythe’, skúpic’ ‘to pile up’, skupíc’ ‘to buy up’, sálic’ ‘to grease’, salíc’ ‘to salt’, as well as morphologically contrastive, e.g., nahí ‘leg, foot’ (Gen sg) versus nóhi (Nom pl), rukí ‘arm, hand’ (Gen sg) versus rúki (Nom pl), vysypác’ ‘to pour out’ (imperfective) versus výsypac’ (perfective), to cite a few examples. Stress may pattern differently in inflectional paradigms, as FIXED STEM stress (Type A), as FIXED SUFFIX stress (Type B), and as various implementations of alternating or mobile stress (Types B1, C, C1, and D below).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Belarusian with an empty rule field and there are no existing statements, so there is nothing to contradict. Bethin supplies the type: free (lexically contrastive, edge-independent) stress with paradigmatic mobility, i.e. lexical (unpredictable), and adds the paradigm-pattern inventory and the ongoing gender-linked stress changes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Belarusian has free lexical stress (p. 239: 'languages with free lexical stress such as Belarusian, Russian, and Ukrainian'; p. 240: 'a language with free lexical stress'). Stress is not tied to a word edge or to weight; it is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs muká/múka, kása/kasá) and morphologically contrastive (Gen sg nahí vs Nom pl nóhi). Within inflectional paradigms stress follows one of a small set of paradigmatic patterns: fixed stem (A, the majority pattern), fixed suffix (B), mobile stem-in-sg/suffix-in-pl (C), mobile suffix-in-sg/stem-in-pl (D), and minor types B1, B2, C1. The paper's own contribution is that Standard Belarusian is extending the mobile patterns (C for Decl. Ia masculines, D for Decl. II feminines; neuters default to fixed stem stress) so that paradigmatic stress now signals gender and, in common-gender and a-stem masculine nouns, determines case exponents.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (the only occurrence of 'secondary stress' is in the title of a cited Russian paper, Gouskova 2010).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 242: 'The discussion is based on the standard language; there are some different implementations of stress patterns in dialects (see Kryvitski 2003; Smułkowa 1978).' Fn. 6, p. 245: in polysyllabic stressed suffixes 'the stress always falls on the first syllable, e.g., Instr pl /-ámi/'; minor paradigmatic types B1 (naha, ruka), B2 (krow), C1 (Declension III) and a stressed Prep sg -ú variant (mjad-ú beside mjódz-je). p. 258: unstressed /o/, /e/, /a/ neutralize to /a/ (strong akanne/jakanne), which makes Decl. II -a and Decl. Ib -o/-e citation forms homophonous under stem stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bethin 2022 describes Standard Belarusian (the literary standard); p. 242 notes that dialects show 'different implementations of stress patterns' (Kryvitski 2003; Smułkowa 1978) but does not describe them.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the Cambridge Core text we hold layer under the 'Stress' heading. (2) Deciding source is a 2021 JIPA Illustration (phonetic description with measurements) that relays the standard Belarusian phonetics handbooks; Belarusian free/contrastive/mobile stress is uncontroversial across the tradition. LOT's open repository yielded Dubina 2012, a full dissertation on Belarusian free stress, with record; its introduction (pp. 1-2) and sec. 3.1 confirm contrastive, weight-insensitive, edge-free stress with duration as main cue and no secondary stress (pretonic prominence treated as vowel-reduction/to

sources.quote: Kaip ir daugelio slavų kalbų, baltarusių kalbos kirtis yra dinaminis. Gadino-Barãnovičių baltarusių šnektos šiuo atžvilgiu nėra išimtis, o tokiomis sąlygomis nekirčiuoti skiemenys redukuojami, todėl visada iki tam tikro laipsnio sutrumpėja. Tačiau viduriniosios kartos Ródūnios apylinkių kaimo gyventojų baltarusių tarmėje nekirčiuoti skiemenys sutrumpėja labai nežymiai (silpnai), t. y. išlaikoma lietuviška kirčiavimo prigimtis ir skambesys, nors funkcinio vaidmens tai nebeatlieka.
sources.note: marginal: Contact study of Lithuanian and Belarusian dialects near Radun; notes that speakers with a Belarusian articulatory base lengthen stressed short vowels, reduce unstressed vowels inconsistently and lose the Lithuanian acute/circumflex distinction, so Belarusian stress behaviour appears only as the contact source, not as the object.

sources.quote: 'In East Slavic languages, the position of stress is not limited in any way at all. ... any given word form is always stressed on one and the same syllable, bar accentual variation, but the location of stress cannot be predicted on the basis of the word's syllabic composition.' Belarusian examples: 'rukji 'arms' vs ru'kji 'arm' Gen.Sg; horat vs pa'rat 'show that syllable weight is not a factor'; 'stress in Belarusian is not limited to any particular position or positions in a word; in this sense, it is free ... contrastive, weight-insensitive, and whose position is not fixed relative to word e
